source.title: The Rate-Distortion-Polysemanticity Tradeoff in SAEs
source.authors: Tommaso Mencattini; Francesco Montagna; Francesco Locatello

record.file_problem: Complete and readable; some equations and figure text have minor formatting or OCR corruption.
record.tranche_reason: Tests a related toy-model claim about polysemantic representations under capacity constraints, using an SAE rate-distortion-polysemanticity analysis rather than the original toy-superposition method.
record.gate_note: The synthetic SAE experiments measure polysemanticity and reconstruction as rate and polysemanticity constraints vary. The Gemma SAEBench audit reports proxy-consistency statistics, not direct results on whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or recovered as complete, stable units; those statistics are not catalog rows for the listed versions. The paper discusses superposition and related work, but does not test the near-orthogonal direction geometry or a sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
record.test_reason: The study measures polysemanticity of SAE dictionary atoms against a known synthetic generative process. It does not measure polysemanticity of a network's own neurons or hidden units. It shows that rate- and width-constrained SAEs merge co-occurring concepts into mixed atoms. This is a related but different construct: dictionary latents, not the model's units, so V2/V3 are not tested. The Gemma SAEBench audit asks whether proxy metrics follow the predicted tradeoff. It does not test whether LLM features are spread across neurons or whether SAE features are canonical units, so V4/V5 are not tested. Superposition itself (Elhage et al.) appears only in related work and as background for the data-generating process.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but needs additions. Under toy assumptions (orthogonal concepts, zero biases, binary aligned atoms), the authors argue SAE polysemanticity is an optimal response to concept co-occurrence under sparsity constraints. They hold that it is driven by joint occurrence, not correlation. Enforcing monosemanticity necessarily costs rate or distortion. They also find that existing SAEBench proxy metrics mostly fail a necessary monotonicity criterion, with AutoInterp the most misaligned. They call polysemanticity a data problem.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a formal data-generating process, an SAE rate-distortion-polysemanticity analysis, synthetic sweeps, and an audit of existing SAE proxy metrics; it does not reproduce the original toy-superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Toy results depend on the co-occurrence distribution, rate constraint, and polysemanticity budget. The real-world proxy audit reports different outcomes for TopK and ReLU Gemma SAEs.

fits_no_version.finding: In width/rate-constrained TopK SAEs on a synthetic generative process, optimal dictionary atoms become polysemantic: they bundle co-occurring concepts (hedging/splitting). Enforcing monosemanticity raises rate or distortion, and the premium is governed by co-occurrence probability rather than correlation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latent polysemanticity (relative to ground-truth concepts) is an optimal response to concept co-occurrence under rate/width constraints, so SAE features need not be monosemantic units.

fits_no_version.finding: On Gemma SAEBench SAEs, no proxy metric clearly follows the predicted rate-distortion-polysemanticity direction. AutoInterp is most inverted (TopK V=0.89, ρ=−0.68). Only Sparse Probing and Splitting weakly agree on TopK.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Common SAE interpretability proxies do not track ground-truth-style polysemanticity.

record.problems: The strongest theoretical and empirical claims rely on stylized assumptions, including orthogonal concepts, zero biases, and binary/aligned atoms. The synthetic sweep reports 7 seeds but no uncertainty estimates in the text. The real-world audit uses proxy metrics and is not a definitive measurement of interpretability.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The Gemma proxy audit is not included as a claim-version result because it reports whether proxies follow a proposed consistency criterion, not direct outcomes for the listed representational claims.

untested.parts: No near-orthogonal geometry, sparsity-dependent phase transition, or regular geometry is measured in a toy network.
No measurement of neurons in a model becoming polysemantic under capacity pressure, or of importance-based allocation of dedicated dimensions. Only SAE atoms are studied.
Not tested for model neurons. The co-occurrence account concerns SAE atoms only.
The Gemma audit uses pre-computed SAEBench scores to rank proxy metrics. It reports no evidence on features being spread across neurons or recoverable by SAEs.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features. The toy results suggest optimal SAE atoms are mixtures, but in a stylized setting with known concepts.
No comparison of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 link conflates SAE-atom polysemanticity with the capacity account of neuron polysemanticity in the modelled network. Under the same-system rule these rows bear on no version. If the catalogue later adds a version on SAE feature monosemanticity, the rows would fit there. The Gemma audit (Table 2) was correctly left out as rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure whether learned directions are nearly orthogonal or test the claimed regular geometry or sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
Tests capacity-constrained polysemanticity in toy SAEs, not polysemantic neurons in LLMs or importance-based allocation in which important features get dedicated dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than superposition, or whether neuron polysemanticity is evidence for superposition.
The Gemma SAE analysis audits proxy metrics; it does not test whether LLM activations spread features across neurons or whether SAEs recover the claimed sparse features.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features. Its toy setup uses concept directions and binary combinations of them.

rows.subject: width-3 Top-2 SAE
rows.operation_detail: Reports training dynamics on a DGP with orthogonal concepts firing uniformly at probability p = 0.2.

conditions.value: four orthogonal concepts in R2; uniform firing probability p = 0.2

rows.note: The text says the dictionary rotates from a nearly monosemantic initialization to a polysemantic configuration during optimization.
rows.check: Measures SAE dictionary polysemanticity P (atoms vs ground-truth concepts) during SAE training, not neuron polysemanticity in a capacity-limited model. The state holds for the study's own claim only. Note: 'four orthogonal concepts in R2' cannot all be orthogonal; the setup is as stated by the paper.
